gold_reference:
There are three applications:
1. Encoder self-attention: queries, keys and values all come from the previous encoder layer. Every input position can attend to all encoder positions.
2. Decoder self-attention: queries, keys and values come from the previous decoder layer. Future positions are masked, so a position can only attend to itself and earlier positions.
3. Encoder-decoder attention: queries come from the previous decoder layer, while keys and values come from the encoder output. This lets the decoder attend to the input sequence.
evidence_hint: Section 3.2.3, Applications of Attention in our Model.

gold_reference:
The decoder is autoregressive. It must not see future target tokens while predicting the current token.

The Transformer masks illegal future connections by setting their attention logits to negative infinity before softmax. The output embeddings are also shifted right by one position. Together, these measures ensure that the prediction at position i only depends on previously known output positions.

The model adds positional encodings to the input embeddings in both encoder and decoder stacks.

The encodings use sine and cosine functions at different frequencies. The authors hypothesised that this makes relative positions easier to learn because an encoding at a fixed offset can be expressed as a linear function of another position's encoding.

Learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results, but sinusoidal encodings were chosen partly because they might extrapolate to longer sequences than those observed during training.

For sequence length \(n\) and representation dimension \(d\):
Criterion	Self-attention	Recurrent layer
Per-layer complexity	\(O(n^2d)\)	\(O(nd^2)\)
Sequential operations	\(O(1)\)	\(O(n)\)
Maximum path length	\(O(1)\)	\(O(n)\)

The paper says self-attention is faster in computational complexity when \(n<d\).
Refuse to provide a score. The paper reports WMT 2014 machine translation and English constituency parsing experiments, not a GLUE result.
Abstain. The paper provides training hardware and schedule information, but does not give a measured electricity consumption figure in kWh.

The conventional pipeline uses voice activity detection, speech recognition, textual dialogue and text-to-speech.

The authors identify three problems:
- Several sequential components create latency of several seconds.
- Converting speech into text loses non-linguistic information such as emotion and non-speech sounds.
- Explicit speaker-turn segmentation cannot naturally handle interruptions, overlapping speech and interjections.
Moshi uses direct speech-to-speech generation, with separate streams for the user and Moshi. This enables full-duplex interaction without requiring explicit turn boundaries.

Mimi uses a split residual vector quantization architecture.
- WavLM provides high-level semantic information, which is distilled into a separate vector quantizer.
- A parallel residual vector quantizer with seven levels handles acoustic information.
- Their outputs are combined, avoiding the constraint of storing all acoustic information in the residuals of the semantic quantizer.
Its encoder maps a 24 kHz waveform into 512-dimensional representations at 12.5 frames per second. The paper reports a bitrate of approximately 1.1 kbps.

It jointly models the textual representation of Moshi's own speech with its audio.

The text sequence is derived from Whisper transcription, tokenized using SentencePiece and aligned with audio frames using word-level timestamps. It is inserted as the first stream, acting as a prefix to semantic-token generation.

This textual scaffolding improves the linguistic quality of generated speech. Changing the delay between text and audio can also support streaming ASR and TTS.

The paper reports 160 ms theoretical latency and approximately 200 ms in practice.

The 160 ms theoretical latency comes from using an acoustic delay of two during pretraining and one during fine-tuning.

Do not describe both numbers as measured practical latency.
Abstain. The specified paper does not report a TED-LIUM 3 evaluation result. Do not substitute a score from a different dataset.
Abstain. The paper does not establish a maximum concurrent-user capacity. Model latency cannot be used to infer this number.

H-Net has three main components:
- Encoder networks process input sequences.
- The main network operates on the compressed representation.
- Decoder networks reconstruct representations at the original resolution.
Its important property is that the main network can itself be another complete H-Net. This allows recursive construction of multiple hierarchical stages.

The routing module compares adjacent encoder representations through cosine similarity.

It projects the current and previous representations into query and key vectors:
\[
p_t=\frac{1}{2}(1-\cos(q_t,k_{t-1}))
\]

The boundary indicator is one when \(p_t\geq0.5\). The first position is assigned a probability of 1.0 so the sequence begins with a boundary.

The downsampler retains vectors marked as boundaries and discards the others.

The smoothing module addresses the difficulty caused by discrete chunk boundaries, which interrupt gradient flow.

It uses an exponential moving average:
\[
\bar z_t=P_t\hat z_t+(1-P_t)\bar z_{t-1}
\]

High-confidence boundaries preserve their own chunk representation, while uncertain boundaries interpolate with preceding context. This supports differentiable training and reduces alignment errors during upsampling.

The ratio loss solves a different problem: preventing the network from retaining almost all vectors or compressing too aggressively. It encourages the selected fraction \(F\) and average boundary probability \(G\) towards the target \(1/N\).

The authors use bits-per-byte (BPB), which normalises the total negative log-likelihood by the number of bytes. This allows comparison across different input representations.

They also match:
- Bytes per batch, so the models see the same underlying amount of data.
- FLOPs per byte, so their forward and backward compute budgets are comparable.
Abstain. H-Net's dynamic chunking refers to learned sequence segmentation inside a model, not PDF passage sizes or a recommended RAG chunking configuration.
Abstain. The paper describes model scales, data budgets and compute matching, but does not provide an actual cloud-compute expenditure.
